query: How does MLFQ stop a job from hogging the CPU by issuing I/O just before its time is up?
expected_answer: Better accounting, expressed as the rewritten Rule 4, solves the gaming problem: the scheduler tracks total allotment used at a level regardless of how many times the job gave up the CPU, so I/O-before-allotment tricks no longer keep a job at high priority.
expected_facts: Rule 4 tracks allotment used at each level even across I/O
job is demoted once allotment is used up regardless of giving up CPU
gaming is issuing I/O before allotment ends to stay at the same priority and nearly monopolize the CPU

relevant_passages.quote: the following attack: before the allotment is used, issue an I/O operation (e.g., to a ﬁle) and thus relinquish the CPU; doing so allows you to remain in the same queue, and thus gain a higher percentage of CPU time.
Rule 4: Once a job uses up its time allotment at a given level (re-gardless of how many times it has given up the CPU), its priority is reduced (i.e., it moves down one queue).

query: What goes wrong if the priority boost interval is set badly?
expected_answer: The periodic priority boost (Rule 5) works poorly when its period S is mis-set: if S is too high, long-running jobs could starve, and if it is too low, interactive jobs may not get a proper share of the CPU.
expected_facts: Rule 5 boosts all jobs to the topmost queue after time period S
S set too high lets long-running jobs starve
S set too low deprives interactive jobs of a proper CPU share

relevant_passages.quote: Rule 5: After some time period S, move all the jobs in the system to the topmost queue.
If it is set too high, long-running jobs could starve; too low, and interactive jobs may not get a proper share of the CPU.

query: Why does MLFQ start every new job in the top queue, and how does that relate to shortest-job-first?
expected_answer: MLFQ approximates SJF by placing every new job at the highest priority (Rule 3), assuming it might be short; short jobs finish quickly, while longer ones gradually move down the queues.
expected_facts: Rule 3 places new jobs in the topmost queue
MLFQ doesn't know whether a job is short, so it assumes it might be
long jobs sink down the queues, so MLFQ approximates SJF

relevant_passages.quote: Rule 3: When a job enters the system, it is placed at the highest priority (the topmost queue).

If it actually is a short job, it will run quickly and complete; if it is not a short job, it will slowly move down the queu es, and thus soon prove itself to be a long-running more batch-like proc ess. In this manner, MLFQ approximates SJF.
relevant_passages.section: Example 2: Along Came A Short Job

query: Why can't I just put the whole turnstile inside the mutex when building a barrier?
expected_answer: Putting the turnstile (barrier.wait and signal) inside the mutex can cause a deadlock: the first thread blocks at the turnstile while holding the mutex, so no other thread can enter to make count==n true, and nobody unlocks the turnstile.
expected_facts: turnstile placed inside the mutex
first thread blocks at the turnstile while holding the mutex
count==n never becomes true
deadlock results

relevant_passages.quote:
Imagine that the ﬁrst thread enters the mutex and then blocks when it reaches the turnstile. Since the mutex is locked, no other th reads can enter,
so the condition, count==n, will never be true and no one will ever unlock the
turnstile.

In this case the deadlock is fairly obvious, but it demonstra tes a common
source of deadlocks: blocking on a semaphore while holding a mutex.

query: What extra step turns the faulty barrier into one that lets every thread through?
expected_answer: Adding a second signal (barrier.signal()) right after barrier.wait() fixes the deadlock of the non-solution, because each thread passing signals the semaphore so the next waiting thread can pass.
expected_facts: extra barrier.signal after barrier.wait
each passing thread signals the next
non-solution deadlocks with only one thread released

relevant_passages.quote:
But then no one signals the semaphore again and none of the oth er threads
can pass the barrier. This is a second example of a deadlock.

The only change is another signal after waiting at the barrier. Now as each
thread passes, it signals the semaphore so that the next thre ad can pass.

query: What do I need to use so that each thread's updates to the arrival count don't interfere with each other in a barrier?
expected_answer: The shared thread count in a barrier is protected by a mutex semaphore initialized to 1, which gives threads exclusive access so they can increment count safely.
expected_facts: count tracks how many threads have arrived
mutex provides exclusive access to count

relevant_passages.quote:
count keeps track of how many threads have arrived. mutex provides exclu-
sive access to count so that threads can increment it safely.

Again, we have to use the mutex to protect access to the shared
variable count.

query: Why does a waiting customer reacquiring the mutex after waking let more than five people eat at once?
expected_answer: In the non-solution, waking customers must reacquire the mutex at Line 7 and compete with newly arriving threads. If new threads get the mutex first, they can take all the seats, so more than 5 threads can be in the critical section, violating the constraints.
expected_facts: waiting customers must reacquire the mutex after waking
they compete with incoming new threads
new threads can take all the seats first
more than 5 threads can be in the critical section

relevant_passages.quote: But when the customers wake up, they have to get the mutex back , and that means they have to compete with incoming new threads.

mutex . wait () # reacquire mutex
8 waiting -= 1
9
10 eating += 1
11 must_wait = ( eating == 5)

query: What fixes the sushi bar race where departing customers update state, and what does it cost in clarity?
expected_answer: In solution #1 ("I'll do it for you"), the departing customer, who already holds the mutex, updates eating and waiting so newly arriving customers see correct state. The cost is that it is a little more difficult to confirm that the state is being updated correctly.
expected_facts: departing customer updates eating and waiting
it already holds the mutex
newly arriving customers see the right state
harder to confirm state updates are correct

relevant_passages.quote:
The only reason a waiting customer has to reacquire the mutex is to update the
state of eating and waiting, so one way to solve the problem is to make the
departing customer, who already has the mutex, do the updati ng.

A drawback of this approach is that is it a little more diﬃcult to conﬁrm
that the state is being updated correctly.

query: What has to be understood by the programmer for passing the baton in the sushi bar to work?
expected_answer: The "Pass the baton" solution only works if the programmer understands and documents that the signaling thread hands the mutex to the waiting thread, since semaphore semantics do not enforce this transfer.
expected_facts: mutex is transferred from signaling thread to waiting thread
this is an invariant understood by the programmer
not enforced by semaphore semantics

relevant_passages.quote:
As long as both threads
understand that the lock has been transferred, there is noth ing wrong with this.

Keep in mind,
though, that this is an invariant understood by the programm er, and docu-
mented in the comments, but not enforced by the semantics of s emaphores.

query: What do I do if my push to the server gets rejected because a teammate pushed first?
expected_answer: A git push only works if nobody has pushed in the meantime; if someone else pushed first, your push is rejected and you must fetch their work and incorporate it into yours before you can push.
expected_facts: git push works only if nobody has pushed in the meantime
a rejected push requires fetching others' work first
their work must be incorporated into yours before pushing

relevant_passages.quote: This command works only if you cloned from a server to which you have write access and if nobody has pushed in the meantime.
You’ll have to fetch their work first and incorporate it into yours before you’ll be allowed to push.

query: Why would I pick an annotated tag over a lightweight one, and what do lightweight tags lack?
expected_answer: Annotated tags are stored as full objects with checksum, tagger name, email, date, message and optional GPG signing, so they are generally recommended; a lightweight tag is just the commit checksum stored in a file with no other information.
expected_facts: annotated tags store tagger name, email, date and message and can be signed
lightweight tags keep only the commit checksum
annotated tags are generally recommended

relevant_passages.quote:
This is basically the commit checksum stored
in a file — no other information is kept.

query: How can I get around the awkward way of unstaging a file in Git?
expected_answer: Defining an unstage alias with git config (alias.unstage 'reset HEAD --') solves the usability problem of unstaging a file, making git unstage fileA equivalent to git reset HEAD -- fileA.
expected_facts: an alias can be created with git config
alias.unstage is set to 'reset HEAD --'
git unstage fileA equals git reset HEAD -- fileA

relevant_passages.quote:
For
example, to correct the usability problem you encountered with unstaging a file, you can add your
own unstage alias to Git:

This makes the following two commands equivalent:
$ git unstage fileA
$ git reset HEAD -- fileA

query: Why do users need to be given scripts they copy into .git/hooks, and what do those scripts help them avoid?
expected_answer: Client-side hooks (such as commit-msg) solve the problem of users having their pushes rejected by the server's update hook at the last minute, by warning them before they commit so they can fix problems early.
expected_facts: client-side hooks notify users when they're doing something the server is likely to reject
server-side rejection of pushes is frustrating and requires editing history to correct

relevant_passages.quote: The answer to this dilemma is to provide some client-side hooks that users can run to notify them when they’re doing something that the server is likely to reject.

Having their carefully crafted work rejected at the last minute can be
extremely frustrating and confusing; and furthermore, they will have to edit their history to correct
it, which isn’t always for the faint of heart.

query: Why can't the server-side ACL check be reused unchanged in the pre-commit hook for listing modified files?
expected_answer: The server-side method of listing files via the commit log fails in a pre-commit hook because the commit hasn't been recorded yet, so the file list must instead come from the staging area using git diff-index --cached.
expected_facts: server-side method reads files from the log of commits via git log --name-only
at pre-commit time the commit has not been recorded yet
must use the staging area with git diff-index --cached instead

relevant_passages.quote:
You can pretty easily see what files have been modified in a single commit with the --name-only
option to the git log command (mentioned briefly in Git Basics):

Because the server-side method looks at the log of commits, and, at this point, the commit hasn’t
been recorded yet, you must get your file listing from the staging area instead.

query: Is a pre-rebase hook worth using given that the server already guards against non-fast-forward pushes?
expected_answer: The pre-rebase hook can help you avoid a rebase you'd later have to fix, but it can be very slow and is often unnecessary because the server already refuses non-fast-forward pushes (via receive.denyNonFastForwards) and warns if you don't force with -f.
expected_facts: pre-rebase script aborts rebasing commits already pushed to a remote reference
it can be very slow and is often unnecessary
server is presumably configured with receive.denyNonFastForwards

relevant_passages.quote:
Presumably, the server is already configured with receive.denyDeletes and
receive.denyNonFastForwards to enforce this policy, so the only accidental thing you can try to catch
is rebasing commits that have already been pushed.

The main drawback to this approach is that it can be very slow and is often unnecessary – if you
don’t try to force the push with -f, the server will warn you and not accept the push.

query: Why can most git history subcommands run in a bare repository, and which one can't?
expected_answer: Most git-history subcommands work in a bare repository because they don't need the index or worktree, but fixup is the exception because it reads staged changes from the index, so it needs an index in place.
expected_facts: most subcommands don't touch the index or worktree
fixup reads staged changes from the index
fixup is the exception in bare repositories

relevant_passages.quote:
Most subcommands of linkgit:git-history[1] can work in a bare repository as
  they do not need to touch either the index or the worktree. The `fixup`
  subcommand is an exception to this, as it reads staged changes from the index.

Apply the currently staged changes to the specified commit. This is
	similar in nature to `git commit --fixup=<commit>` followed by `git
	rebase --autosquash <commit>~`.

query: What should I use when my history contains merges and I want to rewrite it?
expected_answer: git history is a bad choice when the history contains merges, since it does not yet support them; git rebase with the `--rebase-merges` flag should be used instead.
expected_facts: git history does not work with histories containing merges
git rebase with --rebase-merges is the alternative

relevant_passages.quote:
This command does not (yet) work with histories that contain merges. You
should use linkgit:git-rebase[1] with the `--rebase-merges` flag instead.

Use linkgit:git-rebase[1] if you want to reapply a range of commits onto a
different base, or interactive rebases if you want to edit a range of commits
at once.

query: Why can't git history perform rewrites that would cause conflicts, and what could change that?
expected_answer: git history gives up support for operations that can produce merge conflicts, by design, because history rewrites are not meant to be stateful; this could be lifted if Git learns first-class conflicts.
expected_facts: operations that can cause merge conflicts are unsupported by design
rewrites are not intended to be stateful
could change if Git gets first-class conflicts

relevant_passages.quote:
Furthermore, the command does not support operations that can result in merge
conflicts. This limitation is by design as history rewrites are not intended to
be stateful operations.

If replaying any descendant would result in a conflict, the command aborts
with an error.

query: What should I read instead of the old rate property when checking my rate limit?
expected_answer: The deprecated `rate` property is removed from the rate limit endpoint because it duplicates `resources.core`; integrations should read rate limit information from `resources.core` instead.
expected_facts: `rate` property is removed from the rate limit endpoint
it duplicates information in `resources.core`
migrate by reading from `resources.core`

relevant_passages.quote:
The `rate` property has been deprecated since 2021 and duplicates information
  available in the `resources.core` property.

To migrate, update your integration
  to read rate limit information from `resources.core` instead of `rate`.

query: Why did the beta media type removal lead to deprecating the user and master_branch response properties?
expected_answer: Remnants of the officially deprecated `beta` media type still modify response payloads, so deprecating its support causes properties like `user` (replaced by `owner`) and `master_branch` (replaced by `default_branch`) to be deprecated.
expected_facts: `beta` media type deprecated in 2014 but remnants still modify response payloads
`user` replaced by `owner`
`master_branch` replaced by `default_branch`

relevant_passages.quote:
This media type was officially deprecated in 2014. However, there are still remnants
  of its use that modify response payloads.
`master_branch` response property, replaced by `default_branch`

query: How do I get the attestation bundle now that it's gone from list responses?
expected_answer: The `bundle` field is removed from attestation list and bulk-list responses, and you use `bundle_url` to retrieve the attestation bundle.
expected_facts: `bundle` removed from attestation list and bulk-list responses
use `bundle_url` to retrieve the bundle

query: What replaces the singular assignee field when creating or reading issues and pull requests?
expected_answer: The singular `assignee` field is removed because it duplicates the `assignees` array; integrations should use the `assignees` array for both request parameters and response reading.
expected_facts: singular `assignee` field removed
`assignees` array replaces it
singular field duplicates the array

relevant_passages.quote:
The singular `assignee` field has been marked as "closing down" for years and
  duplicates information available in the `assignees` array.

Use the `assignees` array parameter instead of the singular `assignee`
    parameter when creating or updating Issues.

query: Why did the SARIF response Content-Type change when requesting application/sarif+json?
expected_answer: Setting the `Accept` header to `application/sarif+json` incorrectly produced a response `Content-Type` of `application/json+sarif`, so the change corrects it to `application/sarif+json`.
expected_facts: Accept header set to application/sarif+json
Content-Type was incorrectly application/json+sarif
change corrects it to application/sarif+json

relevant_passages.quote: When trying to receive the SARIF upload by setting the `Accept` header to `application/sarif+json` the response `Content-Type` would incorrectly be set to `application/json+sarif`.
This change corrects this so the response `Content-Type` in this case becomes `application/sarif+json`.

query: How does Raft avoid split votes from repeating forever when many servers become candidates together?
expected_answer: Raft uses randomized election timeouts, chosen from a fixed interval, which spread out servers so a single one usually times out first, and each candidate restarts a randomized timeout so a repeat split vote is less likely.
expected_facts: randomized election timeouts chosen from a fixed interval (e.g., 150–300ms)
split votes could otherwise repeat indefinitely
candidates restart randomized timeout at start of an election, reducing chance of another split vote

relevant_passages.quote: However, without extra measures split votes could repeat indeﬁnitely.

To prevent split votes in the ﬁrst place, election timeouts are chosen randomly from a ﬁxed interval (e.g., 150–300ms). This spreads out the servers so that in most cases only a single server will time out; it wins the election and sends heartbeats before any other servers time out.

query: Why does Raft make a joint configuration phase part of changing cluster membership instead of switching servers straight to the new configuration?
expected_answer: Switching directly from the old to the new configuration is unsafe because servers can't all switch atomically, so the cluster could split into two independent majorities; Raft instead uses joint consensus, a two-phase approach combining old and new configurations.
expected_facts: direct switch from old to new configuration is unsafe
servers cannot be switched atomically, so two independent majorities may form
Raft uses a transitional joint consensus configuration instead

relevant_passages.quote:
Unfortunately, any approach where servers switch directly from the old conﬁguration to the new conﬁgura-
tion is unsafe. It isn’t possible to atomically switch all of
the servers at once, so the cluster can potentially split into
two independent majorities during the transition (see Fig-
ure 10).

In Raft the cluster
ﬁrst switches to a transitional conﬁguration we call joint
consensus; once the joint consensus has been committed,
the system then transitions to the new conﬁguration.

query: What has to hold about message round-trip time and server failure rate for Raft to keep a steady leader?
expected_answer: Raft's leader election only maintains a steady leader if broadcastTime ≪ electionTimeout ≪ MTBF, so heartbeats reliably reach followers and the election timeout is much smaller than the mean time between failures.
expected_facts: Raft needs broadcastTime ≪ electionTimeout ≪ MTBF to elect and maintain a steady leader
broadcast time should be an order of magnitude below election timeout so heartbeats keep followers from starting elections
election timeout should be orders of magnitude below MTBF so system makes steady progress

relevant_passages.quote:
Raft will be able to elect and maintain a
steady leader as long as the system satisﬁes the follow-
ing timing requirement:

The election timeout should be
a few orders of magnitude less than MTBF so that the sys-
tem makes steady progress.

query: Why does Raft have each leader write a blank entry when it takes over, before serving reads?
expected_answer: Committing a blank no-op entry at the start of a leader's term solves the problem that a new leader may not know which entries are committed, which it must know to serve linearizable reads without returning stale data.
expected_facts: each leader commits a blank no-op entry at the start of its term
a leader has all committed entries but may not know which they are at term start
linearizable reads must not return stale data

relevant_passages.quote: Raft handles this by having each leader com- mit a blank no-op entry into the log at the start of its term.
Lin- earizable reads must not return stale data, and Raft needs two extra precautions to guarantee this without using the log.

query: What goes wrong if election timeouts are lowered too far to cut downtime after a leader crash?
expected_answer: Reducing election timeouts shortens downtime, but lowering them too far violates Raft's timing requirement: leaders have difficulty broadcasting heartbeats before other servers start new elections, causing unnecessary leader changes and lower availability.
expected_facts: reducing the election timeout reduces downtime
timeouts below roughly 12-24ms violate Raft's timing requirement
causes unnecessary leader changes and lower availability

relevant_passages.quote: The bottom graph in Figure 16 shows that downtime can be reduced by reducing the election timeout.
However, lowering the timeouts beyond this point violates Raft’s timing requirement: leaders have difﬁculty broad- casting heartbeats before other servers start new elections.

query: What does Raft give up by relying on a strong leader, compared with Egalitarian Paxos?
expected_answer: Raft's strong leadership simplifies the algorithm but precludes some performance optimizations; EPaxos's leaderless approach can achieve higher performance under some conditions, such as lower latency than Raft in WAN settings, at the cost of significant added complexity.
expected_facts: Raft's strong leadership simplifies the algorithm
it precludes some performance optimizations
EPaxos is leaderless and can achieve lower latency than Raft in WAN settings but adds significant complexity

relevant_passages.quote: Raft’s strong leadership approach simpliﬁes the algo- rithm, but it precludes some performance optimizations.
Because any server may commit commands, EPaxos balances load well between servers and is able to achieve lower latency than Raft in W AN settings.

query: What do you give up by adding an index to speed up data access?
expected_answer: An index gives faster reads at the cost of increased storage overhead and slower writes, since you must both write the data and update the index.
expected_facts: an index speeds up reads
an index increases storage overhead
an index slows writes because the index must also be updated

relevant_passages.quote:
An index makes the trade-offs of
increased storage overhead and slower writes (since you must both
write the data and update the index) for the benefit of faster reads.

Using an index to access your data quickly is a well-known strategy
for optimizing data access performance; probably the most well known 
when it comes to databases.

query: Why does putting a separate cache on each request node lead to more misses when requests are spread across nodes, and what fixes it?
expected_answer: If the load balancer randomly distributes requests, the same request goes to different nodes and increases cache misses with per-node caches; global caches and distributed caches are the two ways to overcome this.
expected_facts: per-node caches with randomly distributed requests increase cache misses
global caches and distributed caches overcome the problem

relevant_passages.quote:
However, if your load
balancer randomly distributes requests across the nodes, the same
request will go to different nodes, thus increasing cache misses. Two
choices for overcoming this hurdle are global caches and distributed
caches.

A global cache is just as it sounds: all the nodes use the same single cache
space.

Typically the cache is divided up
using a consistent hashing function, such that if a request node is
looking for a certain piece of data it can quickly know where to look
within the distributed cache to determine if that data is
available.

query: When does serving reads and writes of images from one server stop working well?
expected_answer: A single server handling both reads and writes breaks down under heavy use, because writes hold open connections for the whole upload and can consume the web server's limited simultaneous connections (around 500 by default), slowing reads.
expected_facts: one server handles both uploads and retrievals
web servers have an upper limit on simultaneous connections
writes keep connections open for the duration of the upload and can consume all of them in high traffic

relevant_passages.quote:
Another potential problem with this design is that a web server like
Apache or lighttpd typically has an upper limit on the number of
simultaneous connections it can maintain
(defaults are around 500, but can go much higher) and in
high traffic, writes can quickly consume all of those.

In our example, all requests to upload and retrieve images are
processed by the same server; however, as the system needs to
scale it makes sense to break out these two functions into
their own services.

query: What goes wrong with shopping carts when a load balancer sends a returning user to a different node, and what's the catch with the usual workaround?
expected_answer: Making sessions sticky so a user always reaches the same node keeps their shopping cart contents consistent, but it makes it very hard to use reliability features like automatic failover.
expected_facts: sticky sessions route the user to the same node
sticky sessions keep cart contents available
sticky sessions make it hard to use automatic failover

relevant_passages.quote:
One way
around this can be to make sessions sticky so that the user is always
routed to the same node, but then it is very hard to take advantage of
some reliability features like automatic failover.

All of these algorithms allow traffic and
requests to be distributed, and can provide helpful reliability tools
like automatic failover, or automatic removal of a bad node (such as
when it becomes unresponsive).

query: Why doesn't just adding more servers fix clients waiting on slow requests?
expected_answer: Adding servers does not fix synchronous waiting, because even with load balancing it is extremely difficult to distribute work evenly and fairly; the problem is solved by queues, which abstract the client's request from the work performed.
expected_facts: adding servers does not solve synchronous waiting
even fair work distribution is extremely difficult with load balancing
queues abstract request from the work and let clients proceed asynchronously

relevant_passages.quote:
Adding additional servers to
address system load does not solve the problem either; even with
effective load balancing in place it is extremely difficult to ensure
the even and fair distribution of work required to maximize client
performance.

When a client submits task requests to a queue
they are no longer forced to wait for the results; instead they need
only acknowledgement that the request was properly received.

query: When do load balancers' automatic node removal features end up making an overloaded system worse, and what should be in place to notice it?
expected_answer: Under high load, load balancers remove slow or timing-out nodes, which exacerbates the situation for the remaining nodes; extensive monitoring is needed because overall traffic may look like it is decreasing while individual nodes are maxed out.
expected_facts: load balancers remove slow or timing-out nodes under high load
removal exacerbates load on other nodes
extensive monitoring is important because traffic appears to decrease

relevant_passages.quote:
For example, when it comes to high
load situations, load balancers will remove nodes that may be slow or
timing out (because of too many requests), but that only exacerbates
the situation for the other nodes.

In these cases extensive monitoring
is important, because overall system traffic and throughput may look
like it is decreasing (since the nodes are serving less requests) but
the individual nodes are becoming maxed out.
